The fog didn’t roll in; it descended, a heavy, grey curtain smothering the world beyond the glass. Elias adjusted his spectacles, the lenses fogging instantly with the damp chill of the Atlantic. He was the last of his kind, a relic in an age of satellites and automated beacons, yet the light still demanded a human hand. It wasn’t just about illumination; it was about presence. A machine could rotate, but only a man could witness.

He climbed the spiral stairs, the iron steps groaning under his weight. At the top, the Fresnel lens dominated the room, a jewel of glass and brass that fragmented the beam into a sweeping arc. Elias checked the rotation mechanism, listening for the subtle *click-hiss* that indicated the bearings were true. Silence was his enemy here. Silence meant the machinery had failed, or worse, that the sea had claimed another soul without his warning.

He lit the lamp, a small, ceremonial gesture despite the electric bulb’s reliability. The flame caught, dancing briefly before the electric surge took over, casting a blinding white shaft into the void. Outside, the black water churned, invisible but audible, a rhythmic pounding against the granite foundation. Elias pressed his forehead against the cold
